correctness.rationale: The shared-uniform map is monotone in its real argument, and its expected output is the argument. Thus the coupled expected distance is exactly the distance between the inputs, giving one-step contraction by 1−ε. Banach's fixed-point theorem on finite-first-moment probabilities gives existence and convergence from every integer start; integration of the bounded probability of each state proves uniqueness even among invariant laws with no moment assumption. A fixed finite reflecting interval [−M,M+1] of integers is closed: the affine images of its endpoints are M+1+ε(−M−1/2+2c−cε) and −M+ε(M+1/2+2c−cε), both strictly interior for the stated M and small ε. Writing R(n)=1−n and t(n)=n−1/2+2c, first-step rounding perturbations are reversed in the next reflection, while second-step perturbations are added. Hence the first-order two-step upward rate is (−t(n))_++(t(R(n)))_+ and the downward rate is (t(n))_++(−t(R(n)))_+, including t=0 by the O(ε²) remainder. The upward and downward positivity thresholds are n<1/2+2|c| and n>1/2−2|c|; these give the stated closed interval, all other states transient, and strictly positive interior edge rates, also at staircase thresholds. Dividing the two-step stationarity equation by ε identifies every compact subsequential limit with the unique stationary detailed-balance law; finite support makes this TV convergence. Reflection and evenness follow from the rates. At c=1/2 the ratios give 1:6:6:1 and variance 15/28. For |c|≤1/4 the two affine images of 0 and 1 remain strictly in (0,1), even at equality because the ε² term is inward; the stationary mean is θ_ε, which fixes the exact Bernoulli weights.
residual_risks: The argument fixes real c, uses exact affine arithmetic and fresh unbiased integer rounding, and neither supplies a uniform-in-c rate nor proves convergence of trajectories to a continuous-time process.
